title: 22 NYCRR Part 161 — Use of Artificial Intelligence Technology (New York State Unified Court System)
pub: New York State Unified Court System — Rules of the Chief Administrative Judge
author: New York State Unified Court System

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: Part 161 directly supports the cluster’s core position: existing submission and professional duties keep attorneys and parties accountable for AI-assisted papers, while independent review is required to detect fabricated material. It also reflects the cluster’s identified disagreement over AI-specific rules by opposing mandatory disclosure but allowing courts to adopt discretionary local safeguards.
qs: Since those duties and responsibilities already apply to all submissions, regardless of whether AI tools were used, attorneys and parties should not be required, upon submitting papers, to disclose to the court that they have used AI in the preparation of such papers.

Accordingly, any attorney or party who uses an artificial intelligence tool, as defined in 22 NYCRR 161.2(a), in preparing any paper, as defined in 22 NYCRR 161.2(b), filed in or submitted to this court or served on another party in a case before this court is required to carefully review the paper and independently ensure that it contains no fabricated or fictitious cases, statutes, or other material.

qs: ## Section 161.Appendix A Model Rule Regarding Use of Artificial Intelligence Technology in Preparing Court Papers  Every attorney or party who uses an artificial intelligence (AI) tool in preparing any paper submitted to this court is expected to understand that tool's capabilities and limitations.

Accordingly, any attorney or party who uses an artificial intelligence tool, as defined in 22 NYCRR 161.2(a), in preparing any paper, as defined in 22 NYCRR 161.2(b), filed in or submitted to this court or served on another party in a case before this court is required to carefully review the paper and independently ensure that it contains no fabricated or fictitious cases, statutes, or other material.

kp.k: Courtwide policy permits AI-assisted preparation without routine disclosure
kp.d: Section 161.3 states that attorneys and parties should not be prohibited from using AI to prepare court papers, provided they comply with existing submission duties and responsibilities. Because those obligations apply regardless of AI use, the policy says disclosure of AI-assisted preparation should not be required upon submission. Section 161.1 applies the policy to all Unified Court System courts in civil and criminal cases.
qs: The policy set forth in this Part shall apply to all courts of the Unified Court System, in both civil and criminal cases.

It is the policy of the Unified Court System that the use by attorneys and parties of artificial intelligence tools in preparing papers submitted to a court should not be prohibited, as long as such use is in accordance with the duties and responsibilities that apply to individuals who submit papers to a court.

Since those duties and responsibilities already apply to all submissions, regardless of whether AI tools were used, attorneys and parties should not be required, upon submitting papers, to disclose to the court that they have used AI in the preparation of such papers.

kp.k: Court papers exclude evidence from this regulatory scope
kp.d: The rule defines papers to include briefs, memoranda, affidavits, affirmations, pleadings and other documents prepared for court submission. It expressly excludes materials constituting or offered as evidence, whose treatment and associated AI use remain subject to separate considerations and requirements.
qs: The term "paper" shall mean a brief, memorandum, affidavit, affirmation, pleading, or other document prepared by an attorney or party for submission to a court.

This definition does not include materials constituting or proffered as evidence in the case, as such materials, and the use of AI technology in relation thereto, are subject to separate considerations and requirements.

kp.d: Section 161.4 allows individual courts to implement a part rule governing AI-assisted preparation of court papers and encourages use of Appendix A when they do so. The appendix's specific review, certification and enforcement provisions are presented as a model for discretionary adoption, rather than as a mandatory local rule for every court.
qs: A court may, in its discretion, implement a part rule governing the use by attorneys and parties of artificial intelligence tools in preparing papers submitted to the court.
If a court determines that such a rule is appropriate, the court is encouraged to adopt the model rule set forth in Appendix A of this Part.

kp.k: Model rule expects awareness of capabilities and hallucination risks
kp.d: Appendix A expects attorneys and parties using AI to understand its capabilities and limitations. It identifies fabricated information and fictitious citations as risks, without reporting measured error rates or empirical findings.
qs: Every attorney or party who uses an artificial intelligence (AI) tool in preparing any paper submitted to this court is expected to understand that tool's capabilities and limitations.
Attorneys and parties need to be aware that AI tools, among other risks and limitations, can generate fabricated information or fictitious citations to authority (commonly known as hallucinations).

kp.k: Model rule requires independent human verification of AI-assisted papers
kp.d: Appendix A requires attorneys and parties using AI to carefully review papers and independently ensure that they contain no fabricated or fictitious cases, statutes or other material. Its stated scope includes papers filed with or submitted to the court and those served on another party in a case before that court. It also reiterates that attorneys submitting papers remain bound by professional conduct rules.
qs: an attorney who submits any paper to this court is additionally bound by the Rules of Professional Conduct.

Accordingly, any attorney or party who uses an artificial intelligence tool, as defined in 22 NYCRR 161.2(a), in preparing any paper, as defined in 22 NYCRR 161.2(b), filed in or submitted to this court or served on another party in a case before this court is required to carefully review the paper and independently ensure that it contains no fabricated or fictitious cases, statutes, or other material.

kp.k: Signatures certify verification, with possible sanctions for noncompliance
kp.d: Under the model rule, signing an AI-assisted paper certifies both that the required review occurred and that the paper contains no fabricated or fictitious content. A court finding that the requirement was not satisfied may impose sanctions or other remedial action; the text does not make sanctions automatic.
qs: By signing such paper, an attorney or party certifies that such a review has been conducted and that the paper contains no such fabricated or fictitious content.
If this court determines that this requirement has not been satisfied, such attorney or party may be subject to sanction or other remedial action.

pts.k: The Unified Court System frames AI-assisted preparation of court papers as permissible under existing responsibilities, without routine disclosure of AI use.
pts.d: Section 161.3 states a regulatory policy rather than an empirical finding or market prediction: AI use should not be prohibited when consistent with existing submission duties, and those duties already apply regardless of AI use. On that basis, attorneys and parties should not be required to disclose AI assistance when submitting papers.

pts.k: AI can fabricate information and legal authorities; the proposed model court rule requires human verification and makes noncompliance potentially sanctionable.
pts.d: Appendix A identifies hallucination as a risk, expects users to understand tool capabilities and limitations, and requires careful review and independent checking for fabricated content. Signing certifies that this review occurred and that the paper contains no such content. These are provisions of the model rule that courts are encouraged, but not required, to adopt; the document does not report measured error rates or predict displacement of legal workers.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies on existing legal authority and professional obligations, not empirical evidence about AI performance.
pts.d: The Unified Court System grounds its approach in the duties attached to signing and submitting court papers, citing 22 NYCRR 130-1.1 and 130-1.1a and attorneys' additional obligations under the Rules of Professional Conduct. The hallucination warning is stated without accompanying studies, benchmarks, numerical estimates, or named sanctions cases. Appendix A is a model court rule, not an ABA Model Rule.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The provisions address ongoing court submissions, with no forecast horizon; local adoption of the model rule is discretionary.
pts.d: The supplied document is labelled 2026 and describes a capture dated August 16, 2026, but its rule text gives no effective date or implementation deadline. AI permissibility is conditional on compliance with existing duties. Section 161.4 allows courts to implement a part rule and encourages adoption of Appendix A if they choose to do so. Under that model, review precedes signing and submission, and sanctions depend on a court finding that the requirement was not satisfied.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The policy covers attorneys, parties, and courts throughout New York's Unified Court System in civil and criminal cases, but excludes evidentiary materials from its definition of court papers.
pts.d: Attorneys and parties preparing covered papers are the direct users addressed, including parties acting without counsel. Attorneys have additional professional-conduct obligations. Courts retain discretion over adopting local AI rules. Appendix A extends its verification language to covered papers filed with or submitted to the court or served on another party. Materials constituting or proffered as evidence are expressly left to separate requirements.
